content.p: The Sons of Silence Motorcycle Club is a small, tight-lipped "one-percenter" club that began in the Colorado foothills in the 1960s and grew into one of the better-known outlaw motorcycle groups in the United States. It is smaller than the best-known clubs, yet SlashGear notes that US government literature mentions it alongside them, and a 2003 federal drug assessment ranked it the fifth largest in the country. Over five decades its members have been prosecuted for racketeering, methamphetamine trafficking, kidnapping and illegal firearms. Killings have also been linked to the club in court, in different ways, and the cases below involve individuals, each charged or sentenced on the facts of their own case.

The club does not explain itself. When a Colorado newspaper asked about its history in 2016, an anonymous spokesman replied that the Sons of Silence "don't speak to the media, ever." Most of what is known comes from court filings, police statements and federal threat assessments, and from journalists who have pieced them together.

The club's own German chapters date its founding to 1966 in Niwot, Colorado, a small town near Longmont. The Longmont Times-Call gave 1968 in a 2016 feature, so the year is not settled. The founder, Bruce Richardson, known as "The Dude", was born in August 1939 and served in the Navy from 1958 to 1960. He was living in Longmont when he started the club, the newspaper says. SlashGear suggests he had a model in the Hells Angels and the Outlaws, which by the mid-1960s had been around for years.

Expansion began in 1968, when the first chapter outside Colorado was set up in Iowa. By the time of a 1991 Justice Department report, cited by SlashGear, the club had 17 chapters, with a footprint that included Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana and Minnesota. That report credited an alliance with the Hells Angels for helping the growth in Kentucky and Minnesota. By 2002 the National Drug Intelligence Center counted chapters in eight states, and a year later 27 chapters in 10 states, with a total membership estimated at 200 to 250. HotCars, writing in 2020, put the figure at about 275 members, with at least 30 US chapters. Federal analysts described the structure as much like the Hells Angels, with each chapter governing itself under a president, vice president, secretary-treasurer and sergeant at arms.

The club went abroad in 1998 with a chapter in the Munich area. Its German website lists Freising and Gangkofen as joining in 2001, a South Central chapter in 2002, Viernheim in 2007, Erding in 2010 and Steinach in 2025. SlashGear adds that the German operation has stayed in the centre and south of the country.

Richardson did not remain a quiet founder. SlashGear reports that in March 1972 he and five other members were jailed for assault with a deadly weapon after a brawl in Colorado Springs, and that a newspaper of the day said some of the six were also suspected in plots against police officers. In 1984 he was sentenced to six years in prison for his part in the kidnapping and extortion of a doctor. He is reported to have left the club afterwards and died in 2013.

His successor was Leonard Lloyd "J.R." Reed, a fellow Navy veteran. Accounts differ on the dates. SlashGear says Reed joined in 1975, took over as national president in 1977 and led the club for at least 22 years. HotCars says he joined in 1974, became president ten years after the 1966 founding and held the post for 20 years. Both say he helped create the Colorado Confederation of Clubs in the 1990s, and HotCars adds that he did so with a California attorney, Richard Lester, to improve communication among motorcycle clubs. Reed died in 2003. SlashGear notes that it is unclear who followed him, because the club no longer publicly names its leaders.

Federal agents were watching the Colorado club by the early 1980s. According to SlashGear, the FBI began investigating the chapter in 1981 on suspicion of drug distribution, arrests of several couriers followed in 1983, and six members were convicted in 1985. Operation One Percenter in 1986, aimed at several major clubs and smaller ones, led to 53 arrests across the country.

The largest case came in 1999. An ATF investigation led to the arrest of 39 members, including Reed, according to SlashGear. HotCars says SWAT teams hit 25 club sites across Colorado Springs, Commerce City and Fort Collins, taking 48 weapons, four of them hand grenades, plus 10 pounds of methamphetamine, $25,000 and two clubhouses. HotCars says three major chapters were disrupted. Neither account gives the outcome of each prosecution, and this account does not either. HotCars also reports that a former president, Leonard Ray Shipley, was convicted of methamphetamine offences after a search of his home and received 24 years.

The 2003 Colorado assessment portrayed the Sons of Silence and the Bandidos as the most active outlaw motorcycle groups in the state. It said the club's national headquarters was in Colorado Springs, with other chapters at Denver West, Denver East, Fort Collins, Aurora and Grand Junction, and that members made, moved and sold methamphetamine within the state and in other states, including North Dakota. The Weld County Drug Task Force reported that its local chapter produced and distributed the drug. These are law enforcement assessments, not findings against named individuals.

More than two decades later, the same chapter in Colorado Springs appeared in federal court again. On 16 December 2022, Seburn John Henry IV, 37, whom the US Attorney's Office described as a high-ranking member of the club, was sentenced to 10 years in prison for possessing a firearm as a prohibited person and for possessing methamphetamine with intent to distribute. KRDO reported that detectives had seen him with a handgun during surveillance of a house in June 2021 and found three firearms, two digital scales and 228.88 grams of methamphetamine in a vehicle they stopped later that day.

In November 1994, 14 members or former members of the club were indicted in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, on charges of racketeering, money laundering, conspiracy and violence in aid of racketeering. By July 1996, when two fugitives from that group were arrested in Washington state, the Spokesman-Review reported that seven of the 14 had pleaded guilty and four others had been convicted after a six-week jury trial. The two arrested men, Jeffrey Gruber and Robert McAlister, were still wanted at that point and were described as having ties to the club. Federal authorities said the club then had chapters in at least eight states and links to the Hells Angels.

The alliance with the Hells Angels was driven, according to the 2002 federal assessment, by the two clubs' shared rivalry with the Outlaws. SlashGear says the Sons of Silence clashed with the Outlaws in Indiana in the 1970s and 1980s as they tried to move into the state, with injuries and deaths on both sides. HotCars says a club member used an AK-47 in 1980 to kill the Outlaws' national vice president in Indianapolis; neither source says who was convicted.

The 2002 North Dakota threat assessment said the club moved small amounts of methamphetamine from Colorado and sold it at retail level in North Dakota, where it had chapters in Bismarck, Fargo, Grand Forks and Minot. Officials told the assessment's authors that the club usually used smaller affiliated clubs to handle street sales, which shielded it from law enforcement.
The state's courts later saw two murder cases in which prosecutors or investigators invoked the club, with different levels of proof.

The first was the death of Jack Sjol, a 58-year-old Williston rancher reported missing on 25 April 2013. A tip from a confidential informant led police to a private dump site, where his body was found on 14 May with bullet wounds to the head, face and left upper arm. At a preliminary hearing a detective said the owner of the site, Issac Steen, had told investigators that Ryan Lee Stensaker confided he and "a couple of his buddies" had been hired by the Sons of Silence to carry out a hit. That was an allegation relayed in testimony, and the jury was not asked to decide it. Stensaker was charged with murder, and after a five-day trial moved to Ward County, a jury took less than three hours on 18 December 2014 to convict him. His lawyer had argued that the evidence was circumstantial and that the state could not place him at the scene. Five others were charged in connection with the case: Steen was convicted of hindering law enforcement and given the maximum five years, and conspiracy-to-commit-murder charges against two others were dismissed.

The second case concerned Amanda Stach Engst, who was killed on the Spirit Lake Reservation on 12 October 2015. Billy Joe Herman of Warwick pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in April 2019. At a sentencing hearing, an FBI agent testified that Herman was an "enforcer" for the club who did "dirty work" for it but did not appear to be a member. Herman, who shook his head during that testimony, told the court he "wouldn't be a member of a group like that." Prosecutors called the killing unprovoked, horrific and prolonged, and Judge Peter Welte sentenced Herman on 21 October 2019 to life in prison. Herman's former wife, Crystal Johnson, is serving 20 years for her part.

On 11 September, prosecutors in Morton County, North Dakota, charged four men with conspiracy to commit murder over the stabbing of a 33-year-old man at a July street dance in Mandan. Court documents said three of the men were members of the club or had an "aspirational affiliation" with it, and an anonymous source told investigators that club members had attacked Hells Angels at the dance. They were charged, not convicted, at the time of that report.

In February 2013 Kansas City police arrested three people, two men and a woman, at a house in the Northland district. FOX 4 reported, citing unnamed sources, that the group was trying to recruit in the area and that meth, marijuana and at least ten guns were found. Officials hoped to file federal charges.

In April 2017 police in Rock Springs, Wyoming, arrested three men identified as club members after a man who said he was an enforcer for a rival club, the Bad 7, was beaten in a bar and had his vest taken. The three faced robbery and intimidation charges at that stage.
